text.p: **BIRTHDAYS**
Australian writer and maritime poet EDWIN BRADY was born in 1869. His works included "Australia Unlimited" and "The Ways Of Many Waters".

Australian socialist and anti-conscriptionist PERCIVAL BROOKFIELD was born in 1875. Known as "JACK", he was jailed for cursing the British Empire and calling BILLY HUGHES a "traitor, viper and skunk". JACK was shot dead while trying to disarm a beserk Russian at South Australia's Riverton Railway Station in
Australian World War One Victoria Cross winner ALBERT BORELLA was born in 1881.
American radio star STAN FREBERG was born in 1926. He was best known for his musical parodies such as "Elderly Man River" and "St George And The Dragonet".
Australian singer LANA CANTRELL was born in 1944.

Australian actor GRAEME BLUNDELL, who leapt to prominence as "ALVIN PURPLE", was born in 1945. He also had significant roles in "Odd Angry Shot" and "Don's Party". He is recognised as a successful theatre director in addition to his acting achievements.

Australian cricketer GREG CHAPPELL was born in Adelaide in 1948. He captained Australia a record 48 times and scored 7,000 runs in Test Cricket. He retired from Test cricket in January 1984 with 24,520 runs to his credit in first-class cricket, including 74 centuries. Despite these achievements CHAPPELL will

probably be remembered for the "underarm decision" when he instructed the bowler (his brother TREVOR) to bowl underarm on the crucial last ball in a match against New Zealand. The underarm bowl was legal, but considered unsporting.
**EVENTS**
1485 : HENRY TUDOR, the future HENRY VII, landed in Wales
at the start of his successful bid to seize the English throne.
1556 : A UFO was reported above Basle in Switzerland.
1782 : The Order of the Purple Heart, a decoration for
U.S. soldiers wounded in combat and for military merit was established by GEORGE WASHINGTON at Newburgh, New York.
1840 : The British Parliament outlawed child
chimney-sweeps. Supporters of the bill waged an exhaustive campaign against the practice, claiming the young boys risked serious accident and misshapen limbs from climbing chimneys.
1858 : The first Australian Rules football game was
played in Melbourne, between Scotch College and the Church of England Grammar School. Scotch College won, with just one goal.
1888 : The serial killer, who became known as "Jack the
Ripper", murdered a London prostitute.
1903 : The New South Wales government set up a royal
commission to enquire into the state's falling birth rate.
1907 : The New Zealand parliament took steps to allow

women to stand as candidates for election. The House agreed to amend the Legislative Council Election Bill to enable women to nominate for election to the Council. New Zealand women won the right to vote in 1893.
1911 : A Queensland canecutters strike threw the industry
into chaos.
1926 : The first British Grand Prix was held at
Brooklands over 110 laps (287 miles). ROBERT SENECHAL won in just over four hours at an average speed of almost 72 mph.
1938 : Influential Russian theatre director, KONSTANTIN
STANISLAVSKY, died. He founded the Moscow Art Theatre and pioneered Method acting.
1942 : First U.S. land offensive of World War Two in the
Pacific started in the southern Solomon Islands on Guadalcanal.
1947 : The balsa raft Kon Tiki ran aground on the Tuamotu

Archipelago 101 days after leaving Peru. The expedition, led by THOR HEYERDAHL was attempting to prove that pre-Incan Indians could have colonised Polynesian islands simply by drifting on ocean currents.
1954 : English doctor ROGER BANNISTER won the mile race

against Australia's JOHN LANDY at the British Empire Games in Vancouver. BANNISTER's time was 3 minutes 58.8 seconds to LANDY's 3 minutes 59.6 seconds. The race reached its climax at the final bend when LANDY looked over his shoulder and BANNISTER
surged past.
1957 : OLIVER HARDY, of LAUREL and HARDY, died of a

stroke at the age of 65. OLLIE was first teamed with STAN LAUREL in 1927 in a comedy short. Their relationship was free of antagonism despite LAUREL's insistence that he be paid twice as much as his partner. While LAUREL painstakingly rewrote scripts and became involved in directing their films, HARDY would head for the race track or the golf course. LAUREL was reportedly devastated by HARDY's death.
1958 : Australian runner HERB ELLIOT broke the world mile
record, clocking 3 minutes, 54.5 seconds. Less than a month later ELLIOT broke a second world record, when he ran 1500 metres and lowered his record by 2 seconds, to 3 minutes 36 seconds.
1959 : Buckingham Palace announced that QUEEN ELIZABETH
II was expecting her third child early in the New Year.
1960 : In Havana, FIDEL CASTRO nationalised all US-owned
property.
1964 : The United States stepped up its action in
Vietnam. President LYNDON JOHNSON received approval from Congress to "take all necessary action" against the Communist regime in North Vietnam.
1970 : The USSR signed a non-aggression pact with West
Germany.
1988 : The head of the French rail network resigned,
after a spate of train accidents in just over a month killed almost 60 people and injured more than 100.
1989 : New Zealand Prime Minister DAVID LANGE resigned

after five years as leader. LANGE said he was stepping down because of ill-health, but it was widely believed that he left after caucus decided to reinstate ROGER DOUGLAS as Finance Minister. DOUGLAS was a hardline opponent of LANGE's economic policy. He was succeeded by GEOFFREY PALMER.
1990 : NELSON MANDELA's African National Congress
suspended a 29-year guerrilla campaign against white rule in a dramatic concession that cleared the way to formal talks on ending South Africa's apartheid system.
1994 : ERNESTO SAMPER was sworn in as President of
Colombia.
1995 : Bosnian government troops crushed resistance by

rebel Moslem forces in the Bihac enclave, opening a corridor to a region where a humanitarian catastrophe had been threatened.
